title: Light in the deep
text: More than three quarters of the animals living below the ocean's twilight line can make their own light. This ability, called bioluminescence, has {{1}} independently dozens of times, which tells biologists it must be useful. And so it {{2}}: light is used to hunt, to hide, to mate and to escape. Anglerfish dangle glowing lures; some squid vomit luminous clouds to confuse pursuers; most remarkably, many creatures use light as a cloak. Seen from below against the brighter surface, any animal appears as a dark shape, so vast numbers of fish and squid shine from their bellies downwards, {{3}} in with the brightness above. The chemistry is remarkably efficient: nearly all the energy is {{4}} into light, unlike a torch bulb, which wastes most of its energy as heat. Fireflies on land play a similar trick, timing their flashes with such precision that entire populations {{5}} in unison. For humans the appeal is practical as well as poetic: the underlying chemistry has been borrowed for medical imaging, and the enzymes that make light have {{6}} one of the most reliable tools in the laboratory, {{7}} researchers to follow infections and tumour growth in real time. The ocean keeps most of its displays to itself, and biologists {{8}} that the great majority of glowing species have never been seen alive by science. What is already known suggests the rest will be worth the wait.

gaps.explanation: 'has evolved independently dozens of times' — arisen through evolution; involve, resolve and revolve are form traps.
'and so it proves' = so it turns out to be the case; the other verbs are formal near-forms with unrelated meanings.
'blending in with the brightness above' — merging so as to go unnoticed; the others describe movement, not camouflage.
'nearly all the energy is converted into light' — transformed from one form to another; confer = award, confine = restrict.
'populations flash in unison' — emit their light together; flush = blush, flinch = wince, flaunt = show off.
'have become one of the most reliable tools' — the present perfect needs the past participle 'become'.
'enabling researchers to follow' — make it possible for them to; ensure takes a that-clause, enforce and endow take different patterns.
'biologists suspect that…' — think something probable; inspect and respect need objects, and prospect is not used with a that-clause.
